## Objective

We want to attach each child to a measure of their parents' income during childhood. That measure becomes a regression cut, alongside district spending quartile and race/gender, so we can ask whether the returns to school finance reform differ by a child's economic standing growing up.

We build this link through tax returns. A child is connected to a parent whenever the parent claims that child as a dependent, and once the link exists we read the parent's income directly from the tax records.

This page is a brief overview of the process and the bugs we hit along the way. Variable and dataset names are kept generic, and all figures below are illustrative rather than actual output.

## Inputs

Two pieces come from Jon's loaders.

The dependents crosswalk (Jon's dependents loader) links each child to their parent, anchored at age 15. For each child it carries the parent's identity and the child's birth year.

The income-history loader (Jon's income-history loader) covers all available years. For each filer and year it gives the income reported on the return and the number of filers on that return.

We match the parents from the crosswalk into the income panel, so each row is a linked parent's income in one income-history year, carried on the child.

## Building the parental-income measure

The pipeline goes from those matched rows to a single income number per child.

1.  Attach each child's birth year to the income rows. The crosswalk is first reduced to one birth year per child so this join cannot multiply rows.
2.  For each income-history year, compute the child's age that year as the income-history year minus the birth year, and keep only the years the child was between 12 and 17.
3.  Convert each return to a per-filer amount by dividing the income reported on the return by the number of filers on it.
4.  Sum the per-filer amounts within each child-year to get the household income that child saw that year.
5.  Average those yearly figures across the ages 12 to 17 window to get one parental-income number per child.
6.  Re-attach the crosswalk details to that one-row-per-child result.

The per-filer division in step 3 is what keeps joint returns from being double counted. A return with two filers contributes half of its reported income per filer, so when step 4 sums a child's linked parents the joint income is not added twice.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Illustrative example (not real data).** A child is claimed at ages 13, 15, and 17. The summed per-filer income in those years is \$50,000, \$60,000, and \$70,000. The childhood parental income is the average across years: **\$60,000**.
:::

## Percentiles and quartiles

The income number is then turned into a within-cohort rank.

Within each birth-year cohort, we rank children by their parental income and convert the rank to a percentile from 0 to 100 by dividing it by the number of children in that cohort. Each child is therefore ranked against others born the same year rather than against the whole sample.

We then cut the percentile into quartiles: at or below 25 is Q1, at or below 50 is Q2, at or below 75 is Q3, and everything above is Q4. This quartile is the parental-income cut we carry into the regressions.

## Bugs we encountered

Most of the trouble came from the collapse-and-join steps, where a small mistake quietly changes the income figures instead of throwing an error.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
**Aggregating in one step instead of two.** Income came out too high for children whose guardians filed jointly. The cause was summing the per-filer amounts across all child-year rows at once. The fix is to sum *within* each year first, then average *across* years. In the example above the correct answer is \$60,000; the one-step version returned roughly three times that.
:::
